claims.text: Pulumi component state migrations let component authors ship an upgrade path with the component itself, so existing infrastructure is preserved when the component's internal design changes.
Pulumi's component state migrations are new (a recently introduced feature).
A Pulumi component state migration translates the saved state of a component and its children before Pulumi works out which resources need to change.

Component authors can change a component's internal design and include the state migration in the same release, and users who upgrade the component get the migration run automatically as part of the normal preview and update.
The Pulumi component state migrations API is experimental and may change.
A GitHub discussion for component state migrations feedback exists at https://github.com/pulumi/pulumi/discussions/24799.
A Pulumi docs page exists at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/components/state-migrations/ (the component state migrations guide) and it covers the callback contract.
The pulumi/examples repository contains an example at aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration with three programs (v1, v2, v3) and the migration code, following a VPC through three versions of code.
A Pulumi docs page exists at /docs/iac/concepts/components/ describing components.
A Pulumi docs page exists at /docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/aliases/ describing aliases.
The legacy AWSX VPC component (`awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc`) manages the VPC, subnets, route tables, and gateways.

In the example's v1 program, the legacy `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component creates a VPC with one isolated subnet, a route table and its association, and an internet gateway, with a security group defined outside the component that refers to the VPC.

Because the security group refers to the VPC's ID, replacing the VPC would require replacing the security group too, as documented in the AWS CloudFormation EC2 SecurityGroup VpcId property documentation.
Without a state migration connecting the old state to the new code, upgrading from the legacy AWSX VPC component to the modern one could replace the VPC instead of keeping it.
The example does not create a database.
A replacement database does not automatically contain the old database's data, so deleting the old database without a backup or data migration could lose that data.
The example's second version (v2) upgrades to the modern `awsx.ec2.Vpc` component while keeping the existing network.
The example's third version (v3) removes AWSX and declares the VPC resources directly with `@pulumi/aws`, with Pulumi still managing them.
Across all three versions of the example, the AWS resource IDs stay the same and the security group continues to use the same VPC.

In the example's v1 state, the legacy component tree is `awsx:x:ec2:Vpc` "vpc" containing `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc`, an `awsx:x:ec2:Subnet` "vpc-isolated-0" (wrapping the subnet, route table, and route table association), and an `awsx:x:ec2:InternetGateway` "vpc" (wrapping the internet gateway).

In the example's v2 state, the modern component tree is `awsx:ec2:Vpc` "vpc" with the `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc` as its child, and the subnet "vpc-isolated-1" (with route table and association nested beneath it) and internet gateway placed under the managed VPC.

In the example's v3 state, the root of the tree is the plain `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc` "vpc" with subnet "vpc-isolated-1", route table, association, and internet gateway beneath it, and no awsx component records remain.

Pulumi state records both physical resources and the components that group them; each record has a Pulumi name called a URN, and managed resources also have an ID from the cloud provider such as an AWS VPC ID.
The legacy AWSX VPC component wraps the subnet and internet gateway in separate components, while modern AWSX removes those wrappers and places the managed resources under different parents.
In the example, the Pulumi name of the subnet changes from `vpc-isolated-0` (legacy AWSX) to `vpc-isolated-1` (modern AWSX).

Pulumi aliases handle changes to a resource's name, type, or parent when its saved state remains compatible, but aliases alone do not remove component wrappers or transfer references to replacement resources, which requires a state migration.
Pulumi's `stateMigrations` resource option is used to register a migration callback on the new VPC component, alongside an alias for the legacy component type.
The example's migration file at aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v2/migration.ts in pulumi/examples contains `migrateClassicVpc`.
A Pulumi state migration callback receives the saved state of the aliased old component followed by the state of its children, and returns an object with `newState` and `successors`.
The `newState` value returned by a Pulumi state migration callback is the complete set of records that should replace the old component and its children.
The `successors` value returned by a Pulumi state migration callback is a map from each old URN that disappears to the URN that takes its place.
The alias on the new component lets Pulumi find the old component so its state can be passed to the migration callback.

The example's `migrateClassicVpc` callback is safe to run again: if the state already uses modern AWSX or plain AWS resources it does nothing, and an unexpected component type raises an error rather than guessing.
The example's `rename` helper copies the saved record and changes its URN, type, and parent while preserving the AWS resource ID and other saved fields, and it moves the subnet under the managed VPC.
The two subnet entries in `successors` tell the Pulumi engine that the old component wrapper and the managed subnet map to the same new subnet record.

Pulumi uses `successors` mappings to update dependencies and resource references elsewhere in the stack, so the security group's reference to the VPC remains valid and connected to the migrated VPC record with the same AWS VPC ID.

In the example's third version, the VPC, subnet, route table, association, and internet gateway are declared directly with `@pulumi/aws`; the migration changes who defines those resources in the program, and their configuration can be adjusted in a separate update.
The modern AWSX VPC component does not support some subnet or routing layouts that users may need.

The example's second migration (v3/migration.ts) removes the AWSX VPC component record and moves the managed VPC into its place; both the old component and its VPC child map to the new VPC record, the VPC keeps its AWS ID, and the other resources remain beneath it.
In the example's v3 program, the VPC registration keeps aliases for both previous component types (legacy and modern AWSX) and both migration callbacks.
Pulumi runs multiple state migration callbacks in order, passing each callback's result to the next callback.
A stack still using legacy AWSX can upgrade directly to the plain AWS version, and a stack already using modern AWSX skips the first migration.
Once both migrations have run, both migration callbacks return no result on later updates.
Keeping earlier migrations registered with a component lets its users skip versions without hand-editing stack state.
After a Pulumi state migration changes saved state, Pulumi compares the new program with that state and calls the provider for any remaining changes.
In this example, preserving resource IDs through the migration does not guarantee an empty preview; in-place updates for provider defaults and tags can still appear.
To try the example, start with the `v1` directory and follow its README, using the same stack, backend, project name, AWS region, and availability zone for each version.
Before each upgrade in the example, `pulumi preview` should show no creates, deletes, or replacements for the existing VPC, subnet, route table, association, internet gateway, and security group.
`pulumi preview` evaluates a state migration without saving it, and `pulumi up` saves the migrated state.

When a component author registers the state migration inside the component implementation, users do not need to write the migration, attach the callback, or edit their stack state; Pulumi runs the migration as part of the normal preview and update.
For an internal component change that keeps the same inputs and outputs, users can keep their existing component calls and do not need to know which resources moved or how saved state changed.
The blog post embeds example-program-snippet shortcodes referencing path `awsx-vpc-state-migration-blog` with files modern-vpc.ts.txt, migration-sketch.ts.txt, and plain-vpc.ts.txt, which must exist.
Pulumi state migration callbacks (the `stateMigrations` resource option) run during both previews and updates when prior state exists for the resource.
Pulumi state migration callbacks (the `stateMigrations` resource option) must be idempotent and must return no result when the resource state no longer needs migration.
Pulumi state migration callbacks (the `stateMigrations` resource option) rewrite resource state without performing provider operations.
A Pulumi component state migration is a pure function that transforms the saved state of a component and its children into the state expected by a new component version.
A Pulumi component state migration callback returns the updated state records and successor mappings.
In a Pulumi component state migration result, each successor mapping connects an old URN that is omitted from the result to the URN of the returned resource that takes its place.
If no migration is needed, a Pulumi component state migration callback returns no result.
The Pulumi `stateMigrations` resource option reference page documents the callback API, at /docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/statemigrations/#callback-api.

The state entries passed to a component state migration callback use the checkpoint resource format documented in the Pulumi developer docs deployment schema (pulumi-resource-state), including fields such as `urn`, `type`, `id`, `parent`, `provider`, `inputs`, and `outputs`.
A component state migration callback that returns no result can remain attached when using Pulumi update plans or targeted updates.
The restrictions on state-changing results of component state migrations (with update plans or targeted updates) do not require removing an already-applied migration.
